# Promoting Electronic Patient‑Reported Outcomes in Quality Measurement

Sahil Sandhu, MSc1, Lisa S. Rotenstein, MD, MBA2,3, and Thomas W. LeBlanc, MD, MA, MHS4

1Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA; 2University of California San Francisco School of Medicine, San Francisco, CA, USA; 3Center for Physician Experience and Practice Excellence, Division of General Internal Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, MA, USA; 4Division of Hematologic Malignancies and Cellular Therapy, Department of Medicine, Duke University School of Medicine, Durham, NC, USA

J Gen Intern Med DOI: 10.1007/s11606-024-08789-5 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Society of General Internal Medicine 2024

E lectronic patient-reported outcomes (ePROs) provide measurement of health status and experience of care directly from patients. Categories of ePROs include healthrelated quality of life, symptom burden and interference, functional status, health behaviors, anxiety, depression, and patient satisfaction. These data can be collected electronically either at the point of care (e.g., clinic-based tablets) or remotely (e.g., text, mobile applications, patient portal). While ePROs were historically used for research, improvements in information technology, mobile health tools, and electronic health records (EHRs) have made ePRO data collection readily feasible today as part of everyday care delivery. However, the opportunity to leverage these data to drive real-world improvements at the patient- and population-level remains untapped. In this Viewpoint, we highlight how routine collection of ePROs can improve the patient-clinician encounter and drive organizational-level learning health system efforts. We then argue that ePROs should be more thoughtfully integrated into the quality movement and outline key implementation considerations. This is particularly timely as the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) announced in February 2023 that they intend to move towards using more ePRO measures across programs as part of their Universal Foundation approach.

MAKING THE CASE FOR HEALTH SYSTEM IMPLEMENTATION OF EPROS

Frontline clinicians can use ePROs to better deliver patientcentered care. Patient symptoms often go underrecognized by their clinicians during the traditional office visit. For example, of patients with coronary artery disease who reported angina in the previous month using the Seattle Angina Questionnaire, 42% were believed to have less or no angina by their physician.1 Compared to traditional symptom

screening by clinicians, patient-reported outcomes can yield better sensitivity and reliability, while helping clinicians spend more time addressing patients’ concerns than identifying them. A randomized clinical trial across 52 community oncology practices showed that electronic symptom monitoring for patients undergoing treatment for metastatic cancer significantly improved health-related quality of life, patient-reported physical function, and symptom control.2

Operational leaders of health systems can leverage ePRO data to generate and apply evidence in a continuous cycle of improvement. In this learning health system approach, ePRO data can be used to measure problems experienced by patient populations and test new interventions. For example, two primary care clinics in Colorado developed a registry within their health system’s EHR to identify and track patients with uncontrolled depression using Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) scores.3 Clinic staff then used the registry to refer select patients to a “Collaborative Care for Depression” intervention involving specialized care managers and mental health specialists. They also used the registry to identify patients with a new or increased dose of antidepressants for whom clinical staff would make outreach calls to assess adherence and side effects, such as suicidality. In addition to informing population-level improvement efforts, aggregate ePRO data can be translated into shared decision-making tools for frontline clinicians. For patients with knee osteoarthritis considering total knee replacement, researchers at UT Austin developed a machine learning tool that uses ePRO scores and clinical variables to provide patients with a personalized report with the likelihood of complications and improvement in symptoms and quality of life. Results from a randomized controlled trial demonstrated significant improvements in decision quality, level of shared decision-making, satisfaction, and physical limitations, compared with digital patient education alone.4

HOW PAYERS CAN USE QUALITY MEASURES TO DRIVE ADOPTION

Despite evidence supporting the role of ePROs in care delivery, uptake by healthcare organizations has been limited. Implementation challenges often relate to feasibility and upfront investments in new capabilities. Health systems

must develop the foundational health information technology infrastructure to collect ePROs through their EHRs and develop tools to translate and report raw ePRO data to allow for accurate interpretation within specific clinical contexts.5 Specific considerations relate to displaying data longitudinally, comparing individual patient data with referencesub populations, and providing guidance on responding to items. Health systems must then allocate adequate human resources to ensure that questionnaires are delivered to and from patients, documented in the EHR, and viewed consistently by clinicians, in the context of busy clinical workflows. One underused tool to incentivize adoption of ePROs is quality measures. While patient-centeredness was highlighted as one of the six domains of quality in the 2001 Institute of Medicine report, Crossing the Quality Chasm, less than 10% of quality measures implemented by CMS programs or endorsed by the National Quality Forum are ePRO measures or patient engagement/experience measures.6,7 More intentional use of ePRO quality measures in value-based payment models has the dual benefit of providing financial motivation to improve ePRO uptake by health systems, while also ensuring that the quality movement better captures patient perspectives alongside other quality measures (e.g., 30-day hospital readmission) to more comprehensively incentivize improved care delivery. Structural measures related to ePRO collection are a strong initial step for both primary and specialty care settings. For accountable care organizations participating in the Medicare Shared Savings Program, CMS adopted a payfor-reporting measure related to 12-month improvement in PHQ-9 scores for patients with depression or dysthymia. Similarly, in its bundled payment model for total hip and knee arthroplasty, CMS factored in successful reporting of pre- and post-operative PRO surveys related to functional status and quality of life into a composite quality score tied to payment. As more health systems adopt ePROs, payers can shift from pay-for-collection and reporting to pay-forperformance, with thoughtful consideration of potential perverse incentives related to system-gaming and treating patients inappropriately or avoiding care of certain populations to optimize patients’ responses.

CHALLENGES RELATED TO QUALITY MEASURE DESIGN AND IMPLEMENTATION

When designing such quality measures, payers should assess important design and implementation questions, including those addressed in the National Quality Forum’s recent technical guidance report.7 Such considerations also extend to accreditation organizations, such as The Joint Commission and the National Committee on Quality Assurance, which can also develop ePRO measures and standards for their quality programs in alignment with payers.

First, there are methodological considerations related to measure properties. These include which domains of patient experience should be prioritized, whether a measure should use data from a single or multiple ePROs, and whether measures are psychometrically sound. For example, studies have shown that patient satisfaction surveys may not be able to demonstrate meaningful differences in care among physicians, especially as efforts to increase mean patient satisfaction scores have largely been ineffective.8 Thus, measures that capture more objective aspects of patient experience, such as symptom burden, functional status, or health-related quality of life, may more likely reflect clinical performance. Second, measure developers must develop quality measures that mitigate clinician and patient-level barriers to ePRO collection and use. ePRO tools used in quality measures should minimize the time and effort for patients completing ePROs and for clinicians administering them. Specifically, measures should be optimized to reduce the number and complexity of items, as well as the health and digital literacy level needed to understand and complete them. ePRO items should be available in multiple languages, as well as culturally adapted and validated within each language offered.7 To maximize utility for clinicians, tools used in quality measures should clearly document how to interpret scores (i.e., specific cut points that warrant clinical intervention and thresholds to determine meaningful change). Measure developers can also consider publishing guides and toolkits with evidence-based implementation strategies to facilitate health system adoption. Third, measure developers must consider technological challenges related to EHR integration and interoperability. For CMS to consider ePRO performance measures in value-based payment programs, standardization of sharable data elements is needed to aggregate data across measured entities. This is particularly important for risk adjustment (so that health systems caring for patients with greater clinical and social risk are not unfairly penalized) and stratification by demographic characteristics (so that health systems and payers can identify and address disparities experienced by specific subgroups). Several EHR vendors have already integrated ePRO data collection and management schemas into their platforms, making our proposition much more feasible than it was even five years ago.

## CONCLUSIONS

ePROs can help improve the patient-clinician encounter and strengthen learning health systems, but have had limited uptake as part of routine clinical care. Thoughtful integration of ePROs into quality measurement and value-based payment models can drive adoption by health systems. Successful implementation will require alignment and collaboration by health system leaders, payers, accreditation organizations, policymakers, EHR vendors, researchers, and frontline clinicians.
